content: This document is an updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2010, which now includes one additional study. Primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures are a type of generalized seizure, distinct from other types such as absence, myoclonic, and atonic seizures. Effective management of tonic-clonic seizures is critical as it reduces the risk of injury and mortality while improving the quality of life. While many individuals achieve seizure control with a single antiepileptic drug, approximately 30% of patients require a combination of antiepileptic drugs due to drug resistance. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of lamotrigine as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. For this update, databases including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS) Web, MEDLINE Ovid, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) were searched on March 19, 2019. The CRS database incorporates records from sources such as the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov. No language restrictions were applied, and the authors also contacted GlaxoSmithKline, the manufacturer of lamotrigine. The review included randomized controlled trials (either parallel or cross-over in design) that investigated the use of add-on lamotrigine in individuals of any age with drug-resistant primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Standard Cochrane methodology was employed, with two independent reviewers assessing trial inclusion, evaluating the risk of bias, extracting data, and grading the evidence using the GRADE approach. The outcomes assessed included: (1) a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, (2) seizure freedom, (3) treatment withdrawal, (4) adverse effects, (5) cognitive effects, and (6) quality of life. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat (ITT) basis, with results presented as risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For adverse effects, 99% CIs were used to account for multiple hypothesis testing. Three studies, involving a total of 300 participants, were included in the review. Two were parallel-group studies, and one was a cross-over study. The studies exhibited varying levels of bias, primarily due to poor reporting of methodological details. Data from the two parallel-group studies (270 participants) were meta-analyzed, while data from the cross-over study were synthesized narratively. Participants receiving lamotrigine were nearly twice as likely to achieve a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to those receiving a placebo (RR 1.88, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.45; low-certainty evidence). However, the results for seizure freedom were inconclusive (RR 1.55, 95% CI 0.89 to 2.72; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, inconclusive results were observed for treatment withdrawal (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.99; very low-certainty evidence) and for individual adverse effects, including ataxia (RR 3.05, 99% CI 0.05 to 199.36), dizziness (RR 0.91, 99% CI 0.29 to 2.86), fatigue (RR 1.02, 99% CI 0.13 to 8.14), nausea (RR 1.60, 99% CI 0.48 to 5.32), and somnolence (RR 3.73, 99% CI 0.36 to 38.90). The certainty of evidence for these outcomes was very low. The cross-over study, which included 26 participants, reported that 7 out of 14 participants with generalized tonic-clonic seizures experienced a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency with add-on lamotrigine compared to placebo. However, the study reported four treatment withdrawals without specifying during which treatment allocation they occurred. Rash (reported in seven participants receiving lamotrigine and none receiving placebo) and fatigue (reported in five participants receiving lamotrigine and none receiving placebo) were the most frequently reported adverse effects. None of the included studies assessed cognitive outcomes. One parallel-group study (153 participants) evaluated quality of life but found no significant difference between groups (P = 0.74). The authors concluded that the evidence provided by this review is insufficient to guide clinical practice. Low-certainty evidence suggests that lamotrigine may reduce seizure frequency by 50% or more in individuals with drug-resistant primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. However, very low-certainty evidence yielded inconclusive results for all other outcomes. As a result, the reliability of the findings is uncertain, and the true effects of lamotrigine may differ significantly. Further research involving larger populations and longer study durations is necessary to establish the clinical utility of lamotrigine in this context.
